Earlier this year, scientist Jeannine Lewis considered reaching out to Canberra pet photographer Ina Jalil to ask about taking portraits of herself and her late mother's dog, Beau.

Login or signup to continue reading

It wasn't the first time Jeannine had considered pet photography, but it was the first time she'd done so since 13-year-old Beau came out of his melanoma surgery with part of his jaw excised.

"With his health issues, it suddenly became so important to get that photo as a keepsake."

Everyone's pet is a special pet. But Beau has been an incredible lifeline for Jeannine and her family since 2013, when her mother, Elizabeth, sought out a companion following her breast cancer diagnosis in 2010.

"It was ten years of on-and-off chemotherapy for Mum," Jeannine said.

In those years, Jeannine was comforted by the knowledge that her mother had a friend with her, all over the house; padding along the hallway with her, burrowed under her covers, on the kitchen table stealing her breakfast.

Beau is a "poochon", a cross between a Bichon Frise and a poodle, a typically friendly and eager-to-please breed. Beau has a more unique streak of mischief in him, tempered by a gentleness: he'll sneak into bed, where he's definitely not allowed, but he moves quietly enough to avoid waking you.

Jeannine fondly remembers her mother's daily ritual, what she called "quiet time". Leant back in her recliner, Elizabeth would flick up the footrest of the seat, where Beau would immediately take his place. They sat, just breathing, enjoying each other's company.

"I remember her specifically saying, 'it's quiet time'."

It was a special, soft-spoken friendship. Beau kept Elizabeth company until she died in 2020, at just 66 years old. He was a "constant anchor" during those last years.

For Jeannine, Beau was a comfort in a different way. She knew her mother had a reason to get out of bed every morning, being responsible for someone else. She wasn't lonely.

Elizabeth died from breast cancer during the COVID-19 pandemic. As her husband worked from home, Jeannine continued to work at the hospital as a pathology scientist as she grieved.
